turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. Smith. Thank you so much for taking the time to see me. Um, I hope I'm explaining this right... it's a little embarrassing to admit, honestly, because I really pride myself on doing a good job. 

Well, I'm an auditor, and I've been having this issue where... I keep starting my follow-up items after big audits, or after these mentorship events I help with, and I have absolutely every intention of finishing them right then and there. I really do. But then, I don't know, days will go by and I'll suddenly find out that the final email never actually got sent, or a review note didn't get saved, or a form just never got completely filled out. 

It makes me look so careless, which I promise I'm really not. I try so hard to be on top of things. Is that... does that make sense as a reason to come in? I just really want to fix it so I'm not letting my team down, and I was hoping maybe you could help me figure out why I keep doing it.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient explicitly describes starting work tasks like follow-up items, emails, and forms, but failing to finish them.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often feel like you have a motor running inside you, or do you find it difficult to sit still for long periods?
turns.patient_response:
A motor? Um... I don't know if I'd use that exact word, because that makes me sound a bit out of control, and I really try to be put-together. But... I guess I do have a hard time just doing nothing. 

Like, on the weekends, I always tell my husband I'm finally going to just sit on the couch and rest. I really mean to. But then I just... I sort of bounce around instead. I'll start the laundry, and then I'll check some emails, and then I'll go for a run, or start planning things for the volunteer work I do... and I don't really stop until I'm just completely exhausted. 

I always just thought of it as being productive and helpful, you know? Is that... is that the kind of thing you mean? I hope I'm answering your question right.

symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient confirms having a hard time doing nothing and constantly bouncing between tasks until completely exhausted, which aligns with being 'on the go' or acting as if 'driven by a motor'.

turns.doctor_question: In meetings or conversations, do you often find yourself interrupting others or finishing their sentences before they've had a chance to finish?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, um... I really pride myself on being a supportive colleague, so it's a little hard to admit this. But... I guess, sometimes, yes? I don't mean to be rude at all, I promise. 

It's just... especially when I'm working with the junior auditors, I'll catch myself jumping into the conversation before they've completely finished speaking. It's like the answer or the next step just feels so incredibly urgent in my head, and I just sort of blurt it out before I can stop myself. I really just want to help them get to the solution quickly, you know? But I always feel terrible afterward because I don't want them to think I'm talking over them or that I don't value their input. 

Does that make sense? I hope that doesn't make me sound like a terrible manager... I really do try to work on it.

symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly states they 'blurt it out before I can stop myself' when an answer feels urgent in their head.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient admits to jumping into conversations and talking over junior auditors before they have completely finished speaking.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at your time in school as a child, did you frequently have similar experiences of struggling to stay on task or feeling like you couldn't sit still in class?
turns.patient_response:
Um... well, it's funny you ask about that. I always thought of myself as a pretty good student, honestly. I mean, I got good grades and everything! But... I guess if I really think about it, my teachers did always have some... feedback for me. 

Even back in elementary school, my report cards would always say that I was bright—which I was really proud of!—but they'd also say I tended to lose my assignments or rush past the smaller details. And, um, they did mention that I talked out of turn sometimes, and needed a lot of reminders to just finish the work in front of me. 

My mom actually still jokes about it. She always says I was the kind of kid who could completely ace a test, but then completely forget to turn in the project that was literally sitting right there in my backpack. 

I mean, I think a lot of kids are like that, right? Just a little eager and forgetful? I hope it doesn't sound like I was a bad kid. I really did want to do well in school.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient notes that teachers said they would 'rush past the smaller details' in school.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient mentions needing 'a lot of reminders to just finish the work in front of me,' indicating difficulty sustaining attention.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes failing to finish schoolwork without reminders and forgetting to turn in completed projects.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly states that their report cards noted they 'tended to lose my assignments.'
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient describes being 'forgetful' and specifically forgetting to turn in projects that were already in their backpack.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient mentions that they 'talked out of turn sometimes' in class, indicating interrupting or intruding.

turns.doctor_question: When you were a child in school, did you find that you were physically restless or unable to remain in your seat when you were expected to?
turns.patient_response:
Um... physically restless? Like, not staying in my seat? 

I... I don't really think so. At least, not in a way that was, you know, disruptive or bad. I was always very aware of the rules and I wanted my teachers to like me, so I tried really hard to be good. 

I don't remember ever just getting up and wandering around the classroom or anything like that. I might have fidgeted a little bit, maybe swung my legs or played with my pencils... but I think that's pretty normal for little kids, right? Just trying to get comfortable? 

I really don't think I was the kind of student who couldn't stay in her seat. I hope that's a helpful answer... I just don't have any memories of getting in trouble for that specifically.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly denies leaving her seat in school, stating she doesn't remember getting up and wandering around.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient denies being physically restless as a child, stating she tried hard to be good and follow rules.

turns.doctor_question: Looking at your daily life now as an adult, would you say that your tendency to fidget or feel like you need to keep moving is something that happens almost every single day, or is it more of an occasional thing for you?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, um... I guess if I'm being completely honest, it probably is an everyday thing? But I really do try to keep it under the radar! I'd hate to be a distraction to anyone else, especially at the office. 

Like, when I'm sitting in long meetings, I'm usually just... tapping my foot under the table where no one can see, or maybe quietly clicking my pen. And I do end up shifting around in my chair quite a bit. Actually, one of my colleagues joked the other day that she can always hear my leg going under the desk... which was a little embarrassing to hear, to be honest. I really try to be discreet about it! 

It's just a little extra energy, you know? Just trying to stay focused on the discussion. I hope that doesn't make me sound unprofessional... does that seem like a normal amount of fidgeting to you?

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient confirms fidgeting every day, specifically mentioning tapping their foot, clicking a pen, and shifting in their chair during meetings.
